extraction_notes.note: One sentence both introduces $\#c(g)$ and states the Möbius-inversion count of exact-symmetry tilings; kept as one definition node since the sentence cannot be split.

Each symmetry-class paragraph identifies $\#c\langle g\rangle$ with a Stanley class/OEIS sequence and quotes a cited product formula; typed as external theorems rather than equations or paper claims, since the formulas are attributed by \cite.

The re-indexing ('inflation') of the cited formulas is the paper's own adjustment; the identification sentences of the $\langle fr\rangle$ paragraph went into the vanishing claim ClP4, while for $\langle r\rangle$ the whole paragraph is TP6.

The two TikZ figures (pairing of triangles along axes) carry only illustration of the parity arguments; captions not made nodes. The intro sentence that product formulas were proven for each symmetry class is background with no specific statement.
The note has no sections and no theorem environments although lemma/theorem/observation are declared; every node is prose, so section fields are empty.

nodes.name: Dimer hex tilings of a hexagon
nodes.statement: The combinatorics of tilings of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$ by $120^\circ-60^\circ$ diamonds of side-length $1$ has a long history, both directly (as a problem of interest in thermodynamic models) and indirectly (through the equivalence to plane partitions \cite{David89}).
nodes.definiendum: tilings of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$
differentia: of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$
nodes.statement_short: Tilings of a side-$n$ hexagon by unit $120^\circ$-$60^\circ$ diamonds (equivalent to plane partitions).

nodes.name: A066931: number of distinct tilings
nodes.statement: However, when this note was written the entry for the number of \textit{distinct} such tilings in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) consisted of little more than a table for $0 \le n \le 4$ and a brief discussion of those values \cite{A066931}.
nodes.statement_short: OEIS A066931 counts tilings distinct up to the hexagon's symmetries.

nodes.name: Dihedral group $D_{12}$ with generators $f$, $r$
nodes.statement: The symmetry group of the hexagon is the dihedral group of order $12$, $D_{12}$, which has the presentation $\langle f, r \mid f^2 = r^6 = (fr)^2 = e\rangle$ where, for our geometric purposes, $f$ (for ``flip'') represents a reflection around a diameter and $r$ (for ``rotation'') represents a rotation by $60^\circ$.
nodes.statement_short: Hexagon symmetry group $D_{12}$ presented by a reflection $f$ and a $60^\circ$ rotation $r$.

nodes.name: Convention: reflection axis through two vertices
nodes.statement: At a group-theoretic level it doesn't matter whether we take the reflection to be around a diameter that passes through two vertices of the hexagon, or through the midpoints of two edges; but for the purposes of this note it is taken to pass through two vertices.
nodes.statement_short: The reflection $f$ is taken around a diameter through two vertices of the hexagon.

nodes.name: $fr$ is Stanley's complementation transform
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, $fr$ then corresponds to Stanley's complementation tranform, so a rewrite may be in order to unify the two presentations.

nodes.name: Subgroup poset of $D_{12}$
conclusions: The subgroup poset of $D_{12}$ contains $16$ subgroups
the poset can be expressed entirely in terms of a handful of parameterised maximal chains
nodes.statement_short: $D_{12}$ has 16 subgroups; its subgroup poset is a union of three parameterised families of maximal chains.

nodes.name: $\#c(g)$ and Möbius inversion for exact symmetries
nodes.statement: If we denote the number of tilings which have at least the symmetries of $g \le \langle f, r\rangle$ by $\#c(g)$ then the number of tilings having exactly the symmetries of $g$ is given by the M\"obius function of the incidence algebra of this poset: $\sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$.
differentia: which have at least the symmetries of $g \le \langle f, r\rangle$
nodes.statement_short: $\#c(g)$ counts tilings with at least the symmetries $g$; Möbius inversion on the subgroup poset gives those with exactly $g$.

nodes.name: Normalisation by coset index
nodes.statement: We then normalise each by its index in $\langle f, r\rangle$, since we want the number of tilings corresponding to a single coset.
nodes.statement_short: Divide each exact-symmetry count by the subgroup's index so each orbit is counted once.

nodes.name: A066931 as Möbius-weighted sum over subgroups
nodes.statement: Thus the desired value is $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \sum_{g \le \langle f, r\rangle} \frac{1}{[D_{12} : g]} \sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$$
conclusions: $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \sum_{g \le \langle f, r\rangle} \frac{1}{[D_{12} : g]} \sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$$
nodes.statement_short: A066931(n) equals the sum over subgroups $g$ of $1/[D_{12}:g]$ times the Möbius-inverted count of tilings with exactly symmetry $g$.

nodes.name: Ten conjugacy classes of subgroups vs Stanley's ten symmetries
nodes.statement: At this point, it is worth noting that although there are $16$ subgroups, there are only $10$ conjugacy groups because the $9$ subgroups which contain only reflections each have three choices of axis / axes. Thus there is no disagreement with Stanley's list of 10 symmetries of plane partitions \cite{Stanley86}.
nodes.statement_short: The 16 subgroups fall into 10 conjugacy classes, matching Stanley's 10 symmetry classes of plane partitions.

nodes.name: Main formula for A066931(n)
nodes.statement: Once we take that into account and work through the numbers, we find that some of the weights cancel out, leaving $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \frac{\#c\langle e\rangle + 3\#c\langle f\rangle + 3\#c\langle fr\rangle +\#c\langle r^3\rangle + 2\#c\langle r^2\rangle + 2\#c\langle r\rangle}{12}$$
conclusions: $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \frac{\#c\langle e\rangle + 3\#c\langle f\rangle + 3\#c\langle fr\rangle +\#c\langle r^3\rangle + 2\#c\langle r^2\rangle + 2\#c\langle r\rangle}{12}$$
nodes.statement_short: A066931(n) is a weighted average of six symmetry-class counts $\#c\langle\cdot\rangle$ with weights 1,3,3,1,2,2 over 12.

nodes.name: MacMahon's formula for plane partitions in a box
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle e\rangle$ is the most studied of the cases, being simply the number of tilings (Stanley's case 1). It is A008793 in OEIS, and has formula $\#c\langle e\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{i!(i+2n)!}{(i+n)!^2}$ \cite{MacMahon16}.
nodes.statement_short: The total number of tilings (OEIS A008793) is MacMahon's product of factorials.

nodes.name: Symmetric plane partitions formula
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle f\rangle$ is A049505, the ``number of symmetric plane partitions in n-cube'' (Stanley's case 2), with formula $\#c\langle f\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(2i)!(i+2n)!}{(2i+n)!(i+n)!}$ (with a change of index from the OEIS entry for consistency with $\#c\langle e\rangle$) \cite{Andrews78}.
nodes.statement_short: Tilings symmetric under the reflection $f$ correspond to symmetric plane partitions (A049505), with Andrews' product formula.

nodes.name: $\#c\langle fr\rangle$ vanishes for odd $n$
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle fr\rangle$ is A181119, ``transpose-complementary plane partitions'' (Stanley's case 6), but there's a slight catch. It is non-zero only for even $n$; there is a simple geometric explanation.
conclusions: It is non-zero only for even $n$
nodes.statement_short: Tilings with $\langle fr\rangle$ symmetry (transpose-complementary plane partitions) exist only for even $n$.

nodes.name: Geometric pairing argument along the $fr$ axis
nodes.statement: The axis of symmetry bisects $2n$ triangles, which must pair up along the axis because otherwise they would be forced to pair with two triangles to maintain the symmetry. But the pairs start at the centre of the hexagon, so if $n$ is odd there are two triangles on opposite edges which can't be paired. (See figure 1).
nodes.statement_short: Geometric parity argument: the $2n$ bisected triangles must pair along the axis from the centre, impossible when $n$ is odd.

nodes.name: Transpose-complementary plane partitions formula (inflated)
nodes.statement: The upshot is that the given formula must be inflated as $\#c\langle fr\rangle(2m) = \binom{3m-1}{m} \prod_{i=0}^{2m-3} \frac{(i+4m)!(2i+2)!}{(2i+2m+2)!(i+2m)!}$ \cite{Proctor88}.
nodes.statement_short: Product formula for $\#c\langle fr\rangle(2m)$, re-indexed from the OEIS entry A181119.

nodes.name: $\#c\langle r^3\rangle$ vanishes for odd $n$
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r^3\rangle$ is, astonishingly, not in OEIS!\footnote{Update: it is now A259049.} It corresponds to Stanley's case 5 (self-complementary plane partitions), and is non-zero only for even $n$, for a slightly different reason.
nodes.statement_short: Tilings with half-turn symmetry (self-complementary plane partitions) exist only for even $n$.

nodes.name: Triangle-count parity argument for $r^3$ symmetry
nodes.statement: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ small triangles in one orientation and $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ small triangles in another orientation. For $\langle r^3\rangle$ we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half. This half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be $n$ triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2). By the rotational symmetry, these $n$ triangles must be paired up, but if $n$ is odd this is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: Counting argument: a half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles that must cross the diameter and pair up under rotation, impossible for odd $n$.

nodes.name: Divide into six large triangles
nodes.statement: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ small triangles in one orientation and $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ small triangles in another orientation.
nodes.statement_short: Count the small triangles of each orientation in each of the six large triangles.

nodes.name: Reduce to a half-hexagon
nodes.statement: For $\langle r^3\rangle$ we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half.
nodes.statement_short: By $r^3$ symmetry it suffices to tile a half-hexagon.

nodes.name: Surplus of $n$ triangles crosses the diameter
nodes.statement: This half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be $n$ triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2).
nodes.statement_short: The orientation surplus forces exactly $n$ triangles to pair across the diameter.

nodes.name: Rotational symmetry pairs them; odd $n$ impossible
nodes.statement: By the rotational symmetry, these $n$ triangles must be paired up, but if $n$ is odd this is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: Rotational symmetry pairs these $n$ triangles, impossible for odd $n$.

nodes.name: Self-complementary plane partitions formula
nodes.statement: For even $n$ we have $\#c\langle r^3\rangle(2m) = \#c\langle e\rangle(m)^2$ \cite{Stanley86}.
nodes.statement_short: Half-turn-symmetric tilings of a side-$2m$ hexagon number the square of all tilings of side $m$.

nodes.name: Cyclically symmetric plane partitions formula
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r^2\rangle$ is A006366, ``number of cyclically symmetric plane partitions in the n-cube'' (Stanley's case 3), with formula $\#c\langle r^2\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(3i+2)(3i)!(i+2n)!}{(2i+n)!(2i+n+1)!}$ \cite{Andrews79}.
nodes.statement_short: Tilings with $120^\circ$ rotational symmetry are cyclically symmetric plane partitions (A006366), counted by Andrews' product.

nodes.name: Cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partitions formula
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r\rangle$ is A049503, which is cryptically described as ``A005130$^2$'' and ``Expansion of generating function $A_{QT}^{(1)}(4n)$''. It corresponds to the cyclically symmetric and self-complementary plane partitions (Stanley's case 9). Note that again we must inflate the sequence (since $\langle r^3\rangle \le \langle r\rangle$ the same argument applies), and when we do so we get that $\#c\langle r\rangle(2m) = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1} \frac{(3i+1)!^2}{(i+m)!^2}$ \cite{Kuperberg94}.
assumptions: since $\langle r^3\rangle \le \langle r\rangle$ the same argument applies
nodes.statement_short: Tilings with full $60^\circ$ rotational symmetry (A049503, CSSC plane partitions) vanish for odd $n$; Kuperberg's product for $n=2m$.

nodes.name: Explicit formula for A066931: baseline plus even-$n$ correction
nodes.statement_short: A066931(n) is an explicit sum of three factorial products, plus three more correction products when $n=2m$ is even.
